column47:
The Department of Middle East Studies (MES) at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, is currently accepting applications to its M.A. program in Arabic Studies.

The M.A. in Arabic Studies at the University of Michigan is a two-year program that prepares students for entrance into a top-tier Ph.D. program in Arabic Studies or a related field; for a professional career in which expertise in the Arab world is a prerequisite; or to complement a professional degree (e.g., law, public policy, business, public health).

The program draws on the strengths of our distinguished faculty in Arabic language, linguistics, literature, and culture, and is enriched by the university’s renowned resources for the study of the Middle East, including the Islamic Studies Program, the Center for Middle Eastern and North African Studies (a Title VI National Resource Center), the an-Najah Arabic language program, and an extensive library collection.

The M.A. program has two tracks:

*   Track 1: Arabic Literature and Culture
*   Track 2: Arabic Language and Linguistics

Students on both tracks are required to complete a total of 30 credits (normally, 10 courses) and an M.A. thesis, an original research project of 30-40 pages written under the supervision of an MES faculty member. The degree requirements are flexible in order to meet the needs and interests of individual students. All students are required to take one MES course on literary and cultural theory and one on the structures of Arabic. Additional coursework is chosen from a list of MES graduate courses in consultation with the graduate advisor. Students who have not had the equivalent of five years of university-level training in Modern Standard Arabic must continue to take Arabic language courses. Students are also encouraged to study a second Middle Eastern language.

MFA students are immersed in a dynamic culture of research and creative exploration, with an emphasis on experimentation and innovation. As a Stamps MFA student, you will pursue your work within a supportive community of peers and a faculty of accomplished artists and designers. The MFA curriculum provides a framework for students to identify and explore their own lines of inquiry, balanced with a range of topical seminars, electives, and opportunities for independent study. Implementation science is the study of methods to promote the systematic uptake of research findings and other evidence-based practices into routine practice, and, hence, to improve the quality and effectiveness of health services. This degree trains students to lead implementation efforts for community-based health interventions and programs. Students will gain skills in community-based participatory research, implementation science, and program evaluation. Graduates of the MS program will be well-positioned to serve as research staff and program managers in community-based organizations, public health departments, health care systems, and other settings where health promotion interventions are delivered. All applicants must apply through the American Association of Dental Schools Application Service (AADSAS). Your AADSAS application must be submitted by October 15. After we receive your verified AADSAS application, we will email you a link to our supplemental application.

Required Prerequisite Courses:
- Biology with lab: 8 semester hours
- Chemistry with lab: 8 semester hours
- Organic Chemistry with lab: 8 semester hours
- Physics with lab: 8 semester hours
- English Composition: 6 semester hours
- Biochemistry: 3 semester hours

All prerequisite coursework must be completed at a regionally accredited U.S. or Canadian college or university.

The Dental Admission Test (DAT) is required for admission to the School of Dentistry. All applicants are required to have taken the DAT within three years of the application deadline. Unofficial DAT scores are accepted and can be uploaded to the supplemental application. Canadian DAT is also accepted.

Three letters of evaluation are required. Letters must be submitted directly to AADSAS by the evaluators. We require:
- One letter from a science faculty member who taught you and gave you a grade.
- One letter from another faculty member who taught you and gave you a grade.
- One letter from a professional such as a dentist you shadowed, a PI from a lab you worked in, a volunteer supervisor, or an employer.

A minimum of 100 hours of dental shadowing is strongly recommended.

Unlike the Ford School’s MPP or MPA degrees, the MS degree provides students with a narrower, more specialized focus on technology policy. Admission to the MS will require a bachelor's degree in a STEM field, or extensive coursework and/or experience in science and technology. The program aims to recruit students from a range of STEM backgrounds, including students in the natural sciences, engineering, and computer/data science, who are interested in policy. The program’s curriculum will provide students with core skills in policy analysis and quantitative methods, as well as a deeper understanding of the institutional context in which technology policy is made. All students will take a common core of required courses, an integrative seminar that will bring in technology policy practitioners and researchers, a three-course specialization in a policy area of their choice, and a course in their area of science/technology. The 12-month program starts in August and is completed at the end of the following July.

To provide a sound base of knowledge about the nature of crime, criminal justice systems, and related institutions of social control.
To promote theoretical understanding and critical assessment of the literature on criminology and criminal justice.
To develop the necessary skills for conducting and evaluating research in the areas of criminology and criminal justice.
